Introduction to Tabular Data and Microsoft Excel

Lesson 5: Activity: Doing Math with Functions

Finally, let’s add all of these numbers together. Instead of using symbols as we might for doing a handwritten equation, we can instead have Excel do the math using a function .

Function

A function here refers to a predesigned operation that Excel can run in a cell (or multiple cells) as long as it recognizes the proper inputs.

The first function we will learn is one that can add multiple cells together, the SUM function.

When you add any text after an equal sign in the text entry area, you will get an autofill function with functions sharing that text. This can make adding new functions faster. This view will also share information about formatting your function, based on the function’s presets.

When you enter an equals sign (=) in a cell, and start typing in the data entry box, the program will start autofilling potential functions that match the typed string of characters. This autofill function is helpful because it has a short cheat sheet for how Excel needs the data formatted to work. SUM reads like this:

<div “backsplash”>SUM(number1,[number2],…)</div>

We can enter in cells manually. So for the subtotal we could write out:

<div “backsplash”>=sum(F2,F3,F4,F5,F6,F7,F8,F9,F10,F11)</div>

Or we can write it out as multiple cells at a time

<div “backsplash”>=sum(F2:F11)</div>

This will give the same output. For my math it read as “8785”. Yours might be a little different depending on the amounts you chose for each item.

Do the same for the H, “Total”, column.

Here is our result

We typed out =SUM(H2:H11) and got a total of 9399.95. Your result might be different if you filled in different numbers for your amounts in a previous exercise.

Finally, we know this is all money—specifically American dollars—so we should format it to follow that.

Select the cells in the Subtotal and Total columns, and press the $ button in the Home, Number interface. This interface is especially helpful if you have numbers that are running into multiple decimal places, or if Excel keeps changing your numbers into dates.

Your final EquationsWorksheet should look something like this.

Changing number format can be a way to address other issues in Excel, including the pesky setting that adjusts fractions to calendar dates.

What you should take away from this first exercise is that Excel has a number of functions which are unlocked by typing an equal sign “=” at the beginning of a cell. There are dozens of different functions which this lesson will not be able to cover. We will, however, teach a few functions related to file naming, data organization, and other humanistic uses of Excel.

Lesson by: Sean Purcell, University of California San Francisco
